lesson_title: The Second Life of a Cardboard Box
hook_text: The box your groceries came in has probably been a box five times already. Here is how.
clip_script: A waste picker pulls a trolley of flattened boxes through Johannesburg to a buy-back centre. Baled, trucked to a mill, tipped into a vat of water the size of a swimming pool. Stir, and the board falls apart into fibre soup, because paper fibres are only tangled, never melted. Screen out the staples and tape. Spread the soup on a moving mesh, drain, squeeze, dry on hot rollers. Out comes new board. Glue a wavy layer between two flat ones and you have corrugated: an I-beam made of paper, hundreds of times stiffer than the flat sheet. Back into a box, back to the shop, back in the trolley. Five to seven trips before the fibres wear out, then fresh fibre tops it up. Each tonne saves seventeen trees, twenty-six thousand litres of water and two thirds of the energy. Seventy percent of South Africa's paper goes round this loop. Keep the pizza grease out of it.
visual_style: Whiteboard loop: trolley, bale, pulper vat, mesh and rollers, corrugated cross-section with liners and flutes, new box, back to trolley; a counter ticks from 1 to 7.
pacing: Collection, pulping, forming, structure, loop count, benefits, one warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and check what is in your class paper bin that should not be.
